appNaverMap.title: Download Naver Map or KakaoMap
appNaverMap.detail: Google Maps is limited by regulation in Korea, so walking and some transit directions are incomplete. These two are what locals use.

tmoney.title: Get a T-money card
tmoney.detail: It works on the subway, buses and taxis, and convenience stores both sell and top it up. On an iPhone, try Wallet > Add > Transit Card first: South Korea is on Apple’s supported list, and whether the card can be added depends on your model and region. If it cannot, buy a physical card at a convenience store.
tmoney.linkLabel: Open Wallet to add a transit card

kakaotalk.title: KakaoTalk is the main messaging app
kakaotalk.detail: Reservations and contacting shops mostly go through it; KakaoT is the one for hailing rides.

cards.title: Cards are accepted almost everywhere
cards.detail: Even small shops usually take them. Keep cash for traditional markets and street stalls.

suica.title: Suica / PASMO transit cards
suica.detail: They can be added to your phone wallet and work for transit and at convenience stores.
suica.linkLabel: Open Wallet to add a transit card

transfer.title: Use Yahoo! Transit or Google Maps for connections
transfer.detail: Japanese rail transfers are complex, and a transit app is the most reliable source for departures and platforms.

cash.title: Still carry cash
cash.detail: Small restaurants, the areas around shrines and some shops take cash only.

grab.title: Use Grab for rides
grab.detail: The price is agreed up front, which avoids most of the haggling and detours of hailing on the street.

cash.title: Mostly cash
cash.detail: Markets and street stalls are almost entirely cash, so keep small notes on you.

grab.title: Use Grab for rides
grab.detail: You can hail both motorbikes and cars, and the price is transparent.

cash.title: Cash first, and watch the note denominations
cash.detail: The dong has a lot of zeros, so check the digits before you pay.

contactless.title: Contactless cards work straight on the MRT
contactless.detail: No separate transit card needed; tap your card at the gate.

octopus.title: Octopus card
octopus.detail: Good for transit and convenience stores, and sold at the airport and MTR stations.

mobilePay.title: Mobile payment comes first
mobilePay.detail: Alipay and WeChat Pay can be linked to an overseas card; cash and foreign credit cards are poorly accepted.

tipping.title: Tipping is the default
tipping.detail: Dining in is usually 15–20%, and a service charge may already be on the bill, so check before you pay.

power.plugLine: The sockets are type {{plugs}}. If your plug does not fit, you need an adapter.
power.voltageLine: Mains voltage is {{voltage}}V. Chargers for phones, laptops and cameras are usually marked 100–240V and work as soon as the plug fits. Anything that makes heat — a hairdryer, a straightener, a travel kettle — needs to say on the body that it supports {{voltage}}V.
power.noteJp: Eastern Japan runs at 50Hz and western Japan at 60Hz; ordinary appliances are unaffected.
power.noteCh: The Swiss type J recess is narrower than usual, and some European adapters will not fit it.
power.noteBr: Brazil runs 127V and 220V side by side. The voltage is usually marked next to the socket, so check once after you check in.
